title: NVIDIA and Jülich Run 104-Qubit Magic State Cultivation Simulation on JUPITER Supercomputer - Quantum Computing Report
gist: NVIDIA and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre ran a 104-qubit simulation of magic state cultivation on JUPITER, Europe's first exascale supercomputer, using 8,192 GH200 superchips and 512 TiB of GPU memory to model leakage and coherent noise. The work validates a fault-tolerant protocol said to cut physical-qubit overhead by up to 90% versus cascade distillation factories. It also extends CUDA-Q's reach into European HPC centres.

themes.theme: Magic state cultivation cuts FTQC overhead

insights.claim: NVIDIA and Jülich simulated magic state cultivation under realistic hardware noise, validating a fault-tolerant protocol that reduces physical qubit overhead by up to 90% compared with traditional cascade magic-state distillation factories.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A 90% cut in non-Clifford overhead pulls forward the qubit count needed for useful fault-tolerant machines, which matters for hardware roadmaps and valuations.
insights.quote: validating a fault-tolerant protocol that reduces physical qubit overhead by up to 90% compared to traditional cascade distillation factories

insights.claim: The simulated protocol moves from a distance-3 color code to a distance-7 hybrid color/surface code with active flag error detection, using 104 qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This makes the cultivation-to-surface-code handoff concrete: hardware vendors whose roadmaps are built on surface codes can adopt cultivation without changing their architecture.

insights.claim: The JUPITER work complements Google Quantum AI's cultivation theory and builds on Google's Willow hardware cultivation demonstration published in Science. Cultivation is becoming a cross-industry standard path to non-Clifford gates.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Google's IP and hardware results are setting the fault-tolerance agenda that others, including NVIDIA, are building tooling around.
insights.quote: directly complements Google Quantum AI’s foundational cultivation theory

themes.theme: Why this needed exascale brute force

insights.claim: Magic state cultivation cannot be simulated with cheap stabilizer-tableau methods, because it involves non-Clifford operations and non-Markovian noise. That is why full state-vector simulation on an exascale machine was needed.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: FTQC protocol validation becomes a real HPC workload, which creates GPU demand inside quantum R&D.
insights.quote: requires tracking non-Clifford operations and non-Markovian noise that cannot be simplified by stabilizer tableau methods

insights.claim: The run used a 45-bit encoded state vector with about 35.2 trillion complex amplitudes. It consumed 512 TiB of aggregate GPU memory (64 GiB per GH200 node) across 8,192 GPUs on JUPITER.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This gives a benchmark for the memory scale that QEC simulation needs, and shows such simulation as a flagship use of sovereign European exascale capacity.

insights.claim: To capture superconducting-qubit leakage into a third energy level |2⟩, the team packed groups of three-level qutrits into binary registers. For example, 5 qutrits need 243 basis states, which fit into 8 bits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Modeling leakage is now part of standard FTQC validation, so superconducting vendors' published error budgets will increasingly be judged on how they handle leakage.

insights.claim: NVIDIA developed and scaled the simulation at its new NVIDIA Accelerated Quantum Research Center (NVAQC) on GB200 NVL72 racks, which cut simulation development timelines from weeks to days before the JUPITER run.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is using Blackwell systems as the staging environment for quantum research, which makes its hardware part of the QEC research workflow.
insights.quote: reducing simulation development timelines from weeks to days

insights.claim: The stack was built on CUDA-Q and cuQuantum (cuStateVec), plus cuBLASMp and cuSOLVERMp for distributed factorization. The project expands CUDA-Q's momentum across European supercomputing hubs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This positions NVIDIA as the default software layer for hybrid quantum-HPC whatever qubit modality wins, a low-risk way to gain exposure to quantum.
insights.quote: expands NVIDIA’s CUDA-Q platform momentum across European supercomputing hubs
